comparator.name: International Development Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: Current BIN handbook: 114 common credits, 24 taught Sociology of Development credits, a 12-credit thesis and 30 open credits. General and fieldwork safety are zero-credit requirements. Thesis entry requires 102 prescribed credits including all first-year courses and mandatory knowledge; this example completes all taught prescribed study, including all four thesis-preparation courses, before the thesis. Dutch-taught full-time bachelor; 2026 entrant route selected by official order.
components: Global Challenges and Communication in a Changing World
Academic, research and personal development skills and career reflection. General safety is an additional zero-credit requirement.
Research Methods in the Social Sciences
Critical Perspectives on Agricultural and Rural Development
Economics Evolving: A History of Ideas of Development and Growth
Economic and Sociological Analysis of Rural Livelihoods
Methods, Techniques and Data Analysis for Field Research
Fieldwork safety is mandatory. Research design, problem analysis and rural-livelihoods study prepare the qualitative and quantitative field-research training.

Required field research in the Netherlands, England or Ireland: proposal preparation, two weeks of individual fieldwork, then analysis and reporting. Complete fieldwork safety and prepare through the field-methods course.
Globalization and Sustainability of Food Production and Consumption
The Sociology of Farming and Rural Life
Complete fieldwork safety. Prior social and development theory and study of agricultural development, political sociology and food globalisation prepare the course.
Planetary Development: Sociological and Anthropological Perspectives

Required 12-credit supervised literature-based research project; empirical research may supplement it. Entry requires at least 102 prescribed credits including all first-year courses, plus at least two of the four named specialisation courses. This example completes all prescribed taught courses before the thesis.
Thirty open credits for a minor and/or individual electives at WUR or another university. No particular package or exchange is required.

routeSelection.basis: The generic target has three equally formal 36-EC specialisations: Sociology of Development, Economics of Development, and Politics and Communication in Development. None is identified as the general route, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected neutrally and independently of UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Development, inequality & sustainable livelihoods
alternatives.labelReason: Examines how inequality, institutions and environmental change shape livelihoods through sociology, economics, policy analysis, colonial and Indigenous histories, farming and mixed research methods.
alternatives.concept: Examines how inequality, institutions and environmental change shape livelihoods through sociology, economics, policy analysis, colonial and Indigenous histories, farming and mixed research methods.
alternatives.distinctness: The broad closest response balances social theory, economic distribution and environmental-development applications. The economics route replaces seven courses; the culture and communication route replaces eight.
progression: Research and disciplinary foundations support later analysis. All formal prerequisites are earlier and each course has a planned offering in its assigned term. Six semesters contain four courses each, including Year-1 Personal & Professional Development.

alternatives.label: Development economics & public policy
alternatives.labelReason: Prioritises economic explanations of distribution and policy: microeconomics, macroeconomics, public and behavioural economics, econometrics and mathematical methods, applied alongside farming, environmental governance and qualitative inquiry.
alternatives.concept: Prioritises economic explanations of distribution and policy: microeconomics, macroeconomics, public and behavioural economics, econometrics and mathematical methods, applied alongside farming, environmental governance and qualitative inquiry.
progression: Research and disciplinary foundations support later analysis. All formal prerequisites are earlier and each course has a planned offering in its assigned term. Six semesters contain four courses each, including Year-1 Personal & Professional Development.
alternatives.distinctness: Economic theory, econometrics, probability, linear algebra and behavioural decision-making replace part of the closest programme’s social and cultural analysis. Seven courses differ from the closest programme and fifteen from the communication route.

alternatives.label: Development sociology, culture & communication
alternatives.concept: Investigates power and social change through sociology, colonial and Indigenous histories, environmental justice, African heritage, media and public communication, supported by qualitative research and statistical foundations.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: International development, inequality, poverty and livelihoods
Development economics, political economy and resource distribution
Politics, governance, international institutions, law and justice
Communication, social change, culture and participation
Statistics, qualitative and quantitative field research, policy analysis and thesis work
adjacent: Development economics and global political economy
Environment, food systems and sustainable development
questions: Why are wealth, food security and opportunities distributed unequally?
How can institutions, rights, communication and participation support fairer development?
How do economic and environmental policies reshape livelihoods and sustainability?

selection.assessment: The closest programme materially addresses inequality, power, livelihoods and environment through social theory, political economy, farming, governance and research. The official economics and sociology/communication interests support sequentially accepted alternatives with distinct economic-method and cultural-communication priorities. All three pass academic and current feasibility gates; stop at the maximum.

trace: Direct economic foundation in markets, allocation and macroeconomic processes for studying distribution and policy.
Direct comparative analysis of institutions, democracy and political outcomes supports explanations of unequal governance and development.
Direct social explanation of stratification, class, race and gender using classical and decolonial sociology.
Direct research foundation: empirical questions, design, surveys, statistical analysis and R support investigation of inequality and development claims.
Direct study of environmental justice, social movements, decolonial approaches and degrowth connects inequality and environmental change.
Direct international-relations theories, North–South relations, colonial legacies and global environmental cooperation support multi-level institutional analysis.
Direct analysis of environmental representation, Indigenous/postcolonial media, risk and public debate connects communication with environmental-development questions.
Direct contemporary social theory for power, modernity, colonial relations, stigma and intersecting inequalities.
Direct socio-legal analysis of law, social change, justice, race and gender; also provides the formal foundation for public international law where selected.
Direct historical investigation of modern global change, colonialism, decolonisation and globalisation supports interpretation of present inequalities.
Direct analysis of climate impacts, agriculture, justice and governance, including stakeholder inquiry, links environmental change to social consequences.
Direct qualitative inquiry: field research design, interviewing, focus groups, positionality, coding and interpretation develop evidence about social relations.
Direct microeconomic analysis of choices, incentives, market outcomes and externalities supports explanation of distribution and economic policy.
Direct public-policy economics of public goods, externalities, taxation, redistribution, welfare and efficiency supports analysis of inequality and intervention.

Direct Indigenous histories of dispossession, colonial power, food sovereignty and ecological knowledge connect development justice to land and livelihoods; reciprocal collaboration informs research ethics.
Direct philosophical and legal analysis of human rights, cultural relativism, dignity and protection supports critical inquiry into development justice.
Direct advanced analysis of civil society, solidarity, trust and collective movements; applies social theory to contemporary social change.
Direct open-economy macroeconomic analysis of growth, international exchange and policy; complementary to specialist development economics rather than its replacement.
Direct comparative history of empire, economic and political domination and colonial legacies supplies historical explanations of unequal global power.
Direct quantitative investigation through regression, OLS/GLS, instrumental variables and inference; supports testing economic explanations with data.
Direct public-policy analysis in globalisation, using sugar and national/international policy arenas; policy memos connect institutions and food-related decisions.
Direct institutional and stakeholder analysis of food, water, energy and climate governance; applied policy advice/evaluation addresses power, participation and sustainability.

Direct farming/food-production and environmental-impact analysis with comparative appraisal of sustainable practices and a literature project; complements, rather than replaces, agrarian sociology and household-livelihoods theory.
Complementary calculus, mathematical modelling and dynamic methods support the economic models and probability work in this quantitative route.
Complementary international legal reasoning about states, treaties, rights and institutions clarifies the legal constraints surrounding global economic and policy relations.
Complementary matrices, least squares and linear-algebra methods strengthen econometric and quantitative model reasoning.
Complementary political philosophy examines legitimacy, justice, welfare and non-European/decolonial perspectives behind economic-policy choices.
Direct behavioural economics examines heuristics, biases, framing and experimental approaches to decisions underlying policy responses.
Direct probability, estimation, inference and simulation develop the mathematical basis for interpreting quantitative economic evidence.
Complementary study of European integration, supranational institutions and policy gives a concrete regional case of international economic governance.
Direct rhetorical analysis, speeches, debate and storytelling prepare critical and effective public communication about contested social issues.
Direct historical inquiry into gender, slavery, health, confinement and activism supports analysis of intersecting power relations; its North American focus is bounded.
Complementary ethical argument, including care ethics, supports evaluation of responsibilities and fairness in social-development inquiry.
Complementary film/media foundations and feminist/postcolonial interpretation prepare critical analysis of how social groups and development issues are represented.

Complementary West African heritage study analyses social meaning, authority, colonial dispossession and restitution; gives a specific cultural-power case rather than general development anthropology.
Direct analysis of media and racial power through archive, participant observation and PhotoVoice/podcast methods supports critical social inquiry and representation.
Direct framing and persuasion applied through sustainability/community projects link communication to social and environmental action.
Direct documentary research, interviewing and ethical representation develop public communication grounded in evidence; no compulsory international placement is claimed.

notes.text: WUR provides a dedicated sequence in development theory, rural households, agrarian change, food systems and supervised field research. UCR offers substantial responses through social theory, economics, farming, environmental governance and communication, while specialist rural-livelihoods theory, integrated development fieldwork and the required thesis remain differences.

audience.programmeDescription: International Development Studies examines inequality, poverty, livelihoods, food systems and environmental change through sociology, economics, communication, law and governance. This Dutch-taught bachelor combines a common foundation with a specialisation, field research and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR programme combines social theory, political economy, farming and environmental governance. The alternatives give greater weight to economic models and evidence, or to culture, social power and communication. WUR retains a more concentrated rural-development and field-research sequence.
